findings.why: Directly under 'Vitamin C 10% Face Serum', this reads as if the serum contains 86% Vitamin C. The 86% is the purity of the Vitamin C content, not the concentration in the bottle.
findings.fix: Say what the 86% refers to, e.g. 'Brighten your skin with Vitamin C 10% (86% pure Vitamin C content).'

findings.why: Claiming a serum targets UV damage implies it repairs sun-damaged skin (a structure claim), and viewers could read it as sun protection. Neither is substantiated on this ad.
findings.fix: Helps fade the look of dark spots and uneven tone

findings.why: 'Fades dark spots' and 'Fights dullness' are unhedged outcome verbs, where brand copy scopes efficacy to appearance.
findings.fix: Visibly fades the appearance of dark spots

tone_read: Short, calm and free of fear hooks, but the clipped benefit list ('Lightweight. Potent. Glow-boosting.') reads closer to category copy than to Minimalist's explanatory style. There's no mechanism explaining how the Vitamin C works.
language_read: The product is named with its concentration (Vitamin C 10%), which is on-brand, but placing '86% pure' beside it risks being read as a second, conflicting concentration. Efficacy verbs are mostly unhedged ('Fights', 'Fades', 'Targets').
